title: First Aid
intro: In a large emergency an ambulance may take a long time, and in a building with no working elevator it takes longer still. This module gets a stocked kit into your home and your bag, gets you into a class, and covers the health problems a long outage brings: heat, cold, carbon monoxide and medicines that need a fridge.
credit: Based on Unit 7 of Oregon's Be 2 Weeks Ready toolkit

actions.title: Learn the three priorities of first aid
actions.why: A fixed order of priorities helps you act when someone is hurt and you feel unsure.
actions.how: Memorize three steps in order. First, keep the person alive: check that they respond and are breathing, call 911, and deal with stopped breathing or heavy bleeding before anything else. Second, stop things getting worse: keep them still, warm and out of further danger, and stay with them. Third, help them recover: reassure them and keep them as comfortable as you can until help arrives.
actions.done: Each adult at home has said the three priorities aloud, in order, without help.
actions.cite_todo: An official first-aid steps page (for example the Red Cross check, call, care sequence) to stand beside the toolkit for the order of priorities.

actions.title: Learn the signs of heat illness, hypothermia and carbon monoxide poisoning
actions.why: A long outage in hot or cold weather makes people ill in ways that are easy to miss until they are serious.
actions.how: Learn the signs for heat, cold and carbon monoxide. Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, thirst, headache, nausea, dizziness, weakness, irritability or passing less urine, so move the person out of the heat, take off extra clothing, cool their head, face and neck with cold water, give frequent sips of cool water and get medical care, calling 911 if none is available. Heat stroke: a body temperature of 103 °F (39.4 °C) or higher, confusion or slurred speech, hot dry skin or heavy sweating, seizures or passing out, so call 911, stay with them, move them somewhere cool, take off outer clothing and cool them quickly with cool water, or with ice or wet cloths on the head, neck, armpits and groin and moving air. Cold: shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech or drowsiness point to hypothermia, and a body temperature below 95 °F (35 °C) is an emergency, so get medical help at once, get the person into a warm room, remove wet clothing and warm the chest, neck, head and groin first. In a baby the signs are bright red, cold skin and very low energy. Warm drinks help if the person is awake, but no alcohol, and nothing to drink for someone who is unconscious; once their temperature rises keep them dry and wrapped, head and neck included. Carbon monoxide: headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain or confusion mean get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside. Write the lists on a card and tape it inside the lid of your first-aid kit.
actions.done: The lists of signs are written on a card taped inside the lid of your first-aid kit.

actions.title: Decide how someone who cannot walk gets down the stairs, and when to wait
actions.why: Carrying a person down a stairwell without training or equipment can injure both the person and the carriers.
actions.how: If you live above the ground floor, agree the plan now for anyone who could not manage the stairs when hurt or ill. When there is no immediate danger, stay where you are and call 911: give the address, floor and unit number, say the elevator is out and the person cannot use the stairs, and send someone down to meet the crew at the entrance. Do not try to carry a person down yourselves unless staying is the greater danger, such as fire or smoke you cannot keep out. Tell building management and two named neighbors in advance who may need this help.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the plan, and building management and two named neighbors have been told who may need help on the stairs.
actions.cite_todo: The cited pages cover calling 911, being ready to stay put, and telling neighbors who can help. An official source for the sentence against carrying a person down the stairs untrained is still needed (for example NFPA's evacuation guide for people with disabilities).

actions.title: Decide where the small first-aid kits will live
actions.why: A kit helps only if it is where the injury happens and everyone knows where to find it.
actions.how: The full kit at home has its place set in U7-07, under Household. Plan a small one for the bag you would leave with and, if you have a car, another small kit for it. Write each location on your household plan and show everyone.
actions.done: Each small kit's location is written on your household plan, and everyone at home has been shown each place.
actions.apartment: With no car, the small kit in your grab bag is the only one.

actions.title: Split bulk first-aid supplies with neighbors
actions.why: Gauze, tape, gloves and bandages cost much less by the large box, and two or three households can split one.
actions.how: Ask two or three neighbors or friends whether they are filling a kit too. Compare lists, buy the large boxes together and split them. Agree who keeps any spare stock, and check the dates together once a year.
actions.done: The large boxes have been bought and split with your neighbors, and one named person holds the spare stock.

actions.title: Read your state's Good Samaritan law
actions.why: Your state's Good Samaritan law says how it protects people who help in good faith, and knowing that makes it easier to step in.
actions.how: Search for "Good Samaritan law" with the name of your state, and read the summary on an official legislature, court or health department website. Note who it protects and on what conditions. First-aid classes teach the same habit everywhere: ask before you help, and treat a person who is unresponsive or too confused to answer as having agreed. This is general information, not legal advice.
actions.done: You have read the official summary, and a note of who the law protects and on what conditions is written down.

region.label: Oregon
region.general: Good Samaritan laws differ from state to state, so read the one where you live.

actions.title: Check the first-aid kit and medicine cabinet and list what you have
actions.why: A kit is only as good as what is in it today, and dressings and medicines go out of date unnoticed.
actions.how: Empty the first-aid kit and the medicine cabinet onto a table. Read the date on every item and set aside anything expired, opened, damp, damaged or unlabeled. Write a list of what is left, with quantities and expiration dates, and keep it in the kit. Take expired medicines to a take-back site (U7-06). Compare the list with the home kit checklist (U7-07) and the family medicine cabinet to see what to buy.
actions.done: Nothing expired, opened, damp or damaged is left in the first-aid kit or the medicine cabinet, and a list of what remains, with quantities and dates, is inside the kit.

actions.title: Get rid of expired medicines safely
actions.why: Old medicines left in the cabinet can be taken by mistake, and most should not go down a toilet or drain.
actions.how: Take them to a drug take-back location, which many pharmacies and police stations have, or use a prepaid mail-back envelope. If neither is available, check the FDA flush list and flush a medicine only if it is on that list. Otherwise mix it with something unappealing such as dirt, cat litter or used coffee grounds, seal it in a plastic bag and put it in the household trash.
actions.done: Expired and unused medicines have been taken to a take-back site or disposed of as the FDA advises.

actions.title: Build your home first-aid kit from the list
actions.why: A kit you built from a list holds what your household will need, and you know where each thing is.
actions.how: Start with an empty box. Use a latching box of about 12 by 8 inches and keep it where every adult can reach it. Fill it from the list below, line by line: every line has a size and a count. Its medicines are lines of the family medicine cabinet (X7-04), so buy each one once: acetaminophen 500 mg caplets, ibuprofen 200 mg tablets, bacitracin, neomycin and polymyxin B antibiotic ointment, hydrocortisone 1% cream, polyethylene glycol 3350 powder and loperamide 2 mg caplets. Add the printed first-aid instructions, and write the date you checked the kit inside the lid. Once a year, replace anything used or past its date.
actions.done: Every line of the list is in the box in its size and count, with printed first-aid instructions, and the date you checked it is written inside the lid.

actions.title: Add your household's own medical items
actions.why: A standard kit holds nothing for the conditions the people in your home actually have.
actions.how: Go through each person and add what they would need within a day: prescribed medicines, an epinephrine auto-injector, an inhaler, glucose and testing supplies, spare glasses, hearing-aid batteries. Ask your pharmacist how each item should be stored, and put a slip in the kit listing expiration dates. Anything a person may need within seconds, such as an auto-injector or inhaler, stays with that person as well.
actions.done: Each person's own medical items are in the kit with a slip listing their expiration dates, and any auto-injector or inhaler is also with the person who uses it.

actions.title: Keep naloxone at home and in your bag, and learn how to use it
actions.why: Naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose while an ambulance is on its way.
actions.how: Keep one at home and one in your bag, and read the instructions on the box once. CDC says naloxone is sold over the counter and comes as a nasal spray or as an injection; ask a pharmacist which product to buy, or ask your health department about free supplies and a short class. Learn the steps CDC gives, and read the ones on the pack: give the naloxone and call 911, try to keep the person awake and breathing, lay them on their side, and stay with them until help arrives. If normal breathing has not returned after 2 to 3 minutes, a second dose may be needed. Keep the one at home in its box beside the first-aid kit, and write its expiration date on the kit's list.
actions.done: Naloxone is beside the first-aid kit and in your bag, every adult can point to it, and its expiration date is on the kit's list.

actions.title: Write a one-page medical summary for each person
actions.why: A responder or a doctor who has never met you can treat you faster and more safely with your details on one page.
actions.how: Print one medical summary worksheet per person and fill it in by hand: name and date of birth, conditions, allergies, each medicine with its strength and dose, medical devices with model and supplier, doctor and pharmacy phone numbers, insurance details and an emergency contact. Keep one copy in a water-resistant sleeve in that person's bag and one at home where a responder would look, such as inside the first-aid kit lid. Update it whenever a medicine changes.
actions.done: Each person has a dated one-page medical summary in their bag and a copy at home.

actions.title: Keep one unopened pack of each basic over-the-counter medicine
actions.why: Pharmacies may be closed or out of reach for days, and a fever or a stomach bug is harder to ride out with nothing in the medicine cabinet.
actions.how: Keep one unopened pack of each of these: acetaminophen 500 mg caplets, ibuprofen 200 mg tablets, cetirizine 10 mg tablets, loperamide 2 mg caplets, calcium carbonate antacid tablets, polyethylene glycol 3350 powder and oral rehydration solution. If children live with you, ask their doctor or pharmacist which medicines to keep, and write each child's dose for their current weight on the medication list (FN-04). The usual two are children's liquid acetaminophen, never for a child under 2 unless a doctor has told you to and given the dose, and children's ibuprofen only for a child aged 6 months or more, each measured with the syringe or cup from its own box. A baby under 12 weeks with a fever is seen by a doctor before any medicine. Infants' ibuprofen drops are stronger than the children's liquid, so a dose written for one is never given from the other (see the family medicine cabinet). Do not give aspirin to a child or teenager unless their doctor says to. Do not give loperamide or any other anti-diarrhea medicine to a baby, toddler or young child, or a cough-and-cold medicine such as dextromethorphan with guaifenesin to a child under 4, unless their doctor says to. Never give honey to a baby under 12 months. For a child with diarrhea or vomiting, ask the doctor about oral rehydration solution and stock what they advise. Ask a pharmacist whether any of these clash with medicines your household already takes. Check the expiration dates every six months. The full list is the family medicine cabinet in Household: every line names its drug, its strength, the label's age limit and one brand.
actions.done: One unopened, in-date pack of each of the seven medicines named here is stored, and each child's dose for their current weight is written on the medication list.

actions.title: Plan for refrigerated medicines in an outage
actions.why: Some medicines, insulin among them, lose strength when they get too warm, and a fridge without power does not stay cold for long.
actions.how: Ask your pharmacist now, for each medicine you keep in the fridge: how long can it stay at room temperature, and what do I do if it gets warm or freezes? Write the answers by hand on your printed medication list. Keep a cooler and several freezer packs or frozen water bottles ready; follow each medicine's storage instructions. In an outage, move the medicine into the cooler, with the freezer packs wrapped in a cloth so the medicine does not touch them, and do not let it freeze: insulin that has frozen must not be used. If the power is off for a day or more, call your doctor or pharmacist about a replacement unless the label says otherwise; a medicine someone cannot go without is used only until the new supply arrives.
actions.done: The pharmacist's answers for each refrigerated medicine are written on your medication list, and a cooler and freezer packs or frozen bottles are ready.

actions.title: Write the cover plan for one adult being away for two weeks
actions.why: Most of this plan assumes every adult is at home, and a hospital stay leaves the home one adult short while the children still need collecting, feeding and putting to bed.
actions.how: On one sheet of paper, write who does what if an adult in your home is suddenly away for two weeks, in the hospital for example: the two local adults who can collect and keep the children (the same names as on the school pick-up list, FN-07), who covers nights, who gives any child's daily medicine and where its written instructions are kept, who feeds the pets, and which neighbor holds a key (FN-18). Ask each employer what paid and unpaid leave you could take and write the HR phone number down. The Department of Labor says the federal Family and Medical Leave Act gives eligible employees of covered employers up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in 12 months to care for a spouse, child or parent with a serious health condition, so ask HR whether you qualify. If a helper would stay in your home, ask your landlord how long a guest may stay. On the back, list the hospital bag: copies of ID and insurance card, the medication list (FN-11), a phone charger with a long cable, glasses, and the health-care power of attorney. If two adults share the home, check that each can pay the essential bills alone, from their own account or through access the bank itself granted, with no shared password (MN-22). Under the federal rule on electronic transfers, a transfer by someone you gave your access to is not treated as unauthorized until you tell the bank, so you can be liable for it. Give a copy of the sheet to the two named adults.
actions.done: The sheet is written, and each of the two named adults holds a copy and has agreed to their part.

actions.title: Build a small first-aid kit for your bag
actions.why: The injuries most likely on the way out, cuts, blisters and sprains, happen far from the kit at home.
actions.how: Fill a small pouch with these 12 items: alcohol wipes, cotton-tipped swabs, antibiotic ointment, an instant cold pack, bandages (adhesive ones and an elastic one), butterfly closures, finger splints, gauze pads, disposable gloves, adhesive tape, small scissors and tweezers. Each person's own medicines and their written list go in the bag as well, in the amount the grab bag list gives. Put the pouch near the top of the bag.
actions.done: The pouch holds all 12 items and sits near the top of your bag, with each person's own medicines and written list in the bag too.
actions.apartment: With no car, this pouch in your grab bag is your only small kit.

actions.title: Find a first-aid course near you
actions.why: Hands-on training with an instructor is the only reliable way to learn skills you will have to use under stress.
actions.how: Look in this order: the Red Cross class finder, your fire department, your city or county health department, your employer's safety team, a local hospital, a gym or community center. Choose a course that covers first aid, CPR and use of a defibrillator (AED) and includes hands-on practice; some put the theory online and the practice in a classroom. Write down the date, price and place of two options.
actions.done: The date, price and place of two courses are written down.

actions.title: Find, book and take a first-aid and CPR class
actions.why: Hands-on practice with an instructor is the only reliable way to learn skills you will have to use under stress, before anyone else can arrive.
actions.how: Look for a class in this order: the Red Cross class finder, your fire department, your city or county health department, your employer's safety team, a local hospital, a gym or community center. Choose one that covers first aid, CPR and use of a defibrillator (AED) with hands-on practice on a manikin and an AED trainer; some put the theory online and the practice in a classroom. If a baby or a child under 5 lives with you, choose a class that covers infants and children, because CPR and choking change with age. Check that it covers making an arm sling from a T-shirt, splinting and buddy-taping a finger, wrapping an ankle with an elastic bandage, CPR, choking, controlling severe bleeding, the signs of shock and the response, and cleaning and dressing wounds. Book it, and invite a neighbor or friend from your building to book the same session. At the class, ask what to do if you are alone and choking yourself, and which wounds need professional care. Afterwards, write the choking steps you were taught inside the lid of your first-aid kit, one set for each age at home, and the signs of shock and the response on the card in your kit. As a check on your notes, the American Heart Association's 2025 guidelines alternate five back blows and five abdominal thrusts for a conscious child or adult who is choking, and five back blows and five chest thrusts for a baby, never abdominal thrusts. The same guidelines no longer teach two-finger chest compressions for a baby: compressions are given with two thumbs and the hands around the chest, or with the heel of one hand. If your class was before late 2025, your notes may be out of date. Once a year, practice the sling, the finger splint, the ankle wrap and a wound dressing at home on an uninjured person, and replace what you use. Practice a tourniquet only on a training one, never on the one kept for real use, and never tighten one on a person outside a class. Check that each kit holds finger splints or craft sticks, tape, an elastic bandage, an emergency blanket and an old large T-shirt, and set aside clean water in your plan for washing wounds. Find the nearest AED to your home and your workplace, often in a lobby, gym or reception, and write it on your household plan. Put the certificate's expiration date in your calendar and rebook before it lapses; many certificates last two years.
actions.done: You hold the class certificate with its expiration date in your calendar, and the choking steps you were taught are written inside your first-aid kit lid.

actions.title: Take a Stop the Bleed course
actions.why: Severe bleeding has to be controlled before help arrives, and in a tall building help takes longer to reach you.
actions.how: Find a Stop the Bleed class through the program's website. You practice the three basic actions it teaches for controlling severe bleeding. Buy a tourniquet or bleeding-control kit only after the class, so you know how to use the one you own, and keep it at the top of your first-aid kit.
actions.done: You have completed the class, and any tourniquet or bleeding-control kit bought afterwards is at the top of your first-aid kit.

actions.title: Take a wilderness first-aid course
actions.why: A wilderness first-aid course teaches how to look after someone for hours or days when no ambulance is coming, which is the situation a large disaster creates.
actions.how: Take a standard first-aid and CPR course first. Then look for a wilderness first-aid course from an outdoor school or outdoor retailer; they usually run for two days. Book one and keep the course handbook with your home kit.
actions.done: You have taken the course, and its handbook is with your home first-aid kit.

actions.title: Practice making an arm sling from a T-shirt
actions.why: An improvised sling supports an injured arm or shoulder until the person can get medical care.
actions.how: After your class, practice once on someone at home: use a large T-shirt to support a forearm against the chest, the way your course or first-aid manual shows. Swap over so everyone has made one and worn one. Keep one old large T-shirt with the home kit for this, and repeat the practice once a year.
actions.done: Everyone at home has made a sling and worn one, and an old large T-shirt is kept with the home kit.

actions.title: Practice splinting a finger and buddy-taping
actions.why: Keeping a jammed or broken finger still limits pain and further damage until it can be treated.
actions.how: Practice on an uninjured hand with a craft stick or finger splint and the tape from your kit, as your course or manual shows. Then practice taping one finger to its neighbor. Check afterwards that each kit holds finger splints or sticks and a roll of tape.
actions.done: You have splinted and buddy-taped a finger once, and each kit holds finger splints or sticks and a roll of tape.

actions.title: Practice wrapping an ankle with an elastic bandage
actions.why: Sprained ankles are among the most common injuries when people walk down dark stairs or over debris.
actions.how: Take an elastic bandage from your kit and practice wrapping a household member's uninjured ankle, following the pattern taught in your course or shown in your manual. Ask them whether it feels firm without being tight, then swap over. Roll the bandage back up and return it to the kit.
actions.done: You and one other person at home have each wrapped the other's ankle, and the bandage is rolled up and back in the kit.

actions.title: Get comfortable with CPR
actions.why: When a heart stops, the person nearby is the only help there is for the first minutes.
actions.how: CPR cannot be learned from a page: check that the class you book includes practice on a manikin and with a defibrillator (AED) trainer. If a baby or a child under 5 lives with you, choose a class that covers infants and children. Afterwards, find the nearest AED to your home and your workplace, often in a lobby, gym or reception, and write its location on your household plan. Refresh the training before your certificate lapses.
actions.done: You have practiced on a manikin and with an AED trainer in a class, and the nearest AED to home and to work is written on your household plan.

actions.title: Get comfortable with helping someone who is choking
actions.why: A blocked airway has to be cleared within minutes, long before anyone else can arrive.
actions.how: Learn the response to choking in a first-aid class, where you can practice on a training vest or manikin. If babies or children live with you, choose a class that covers them, because the method changes with age. Ask the instructor what to do if you are alone and choking yourself.
actions.done: You have practiced the response on a training vest or manikin in a class, one that covers babies and children if they live with you.

actions.title: Get comfortable with controlling severe bleeding
actions.why: Heavy bleeding is the injury where the first few minutes decide the outcome.
actions.how: Take a bleeding-control class such as Stop the Bleed, or a first-aid course that includes it, and practice on the training aids there. Practice only on a training tourniquet, never on the one kept for real use. One maker says its tourniquet is a single-use device and sells a blue trainer for repeated practice; read the instructions that came with yours. At home, handle the real tourniquet and the pressure dressings only enough to know how they open and where they sit in the kit, and replace any sterile dressing you open. Do not practice tightening a tourniquet on a person outside a class.
actions.done: You have practiced on training aids in a class, and you can go straight to the tourniquet and pressure dressings in your kit.

actions.title: Get comfortable with recognizing and responding to shock
actions.why: Shock is a life-threatening drop in blood flow that can follow an injury that looked manageable.
actions.how: In your first-aid class, ask the instructor to go through the signs of shock and the response, and write them on the card in your kit. The plan always starts with calling 911. Check that every kit holds an emergency blanket, which is part of the response you will be taught.
actions.done: The signs of shock and the response your instructor taught are written on the card in your kit, and every kit holds an emergency blanket.

actions.title: Get comfortable with cleaning and dressing wounds
actions.why: A small wound kept clean heals; a dirty one can become a serious infection when clean water and doctors are hard to reach.
actions.how: With clean hands, practice on an uninjured arm using your own kit: open a gauze pad without touching its center, hold it in place, and fix it with tape or a bandage, as your course or manual shows. Set aside clean water in your plan for washing wounds. Ask your instructor which wounds need professional care, then replace what you used.
actions.done: You have dressed an uninjured arm once using your own kit, replaced what you used, and added clean water for washing wounds to your plan.
